<reflection>
We now have two experimental runs: run_1 ([S]=2.0, [cat]=0.01, [P]=0) and run_2 ([S]=5.0, [cat]=0.01, [P]=0). The fitting results after run_2 show a clear top cluster: M11, M19, M17, M18, M14, M20, M12, M16 all have NLL values between -42.65 and -39.13, significantly better than the next group (around -29.9 to -29.5). These top candidates are all deactivation mechanisms, differing in the species involved in the deactivation step. The aim of this turn is to discriminate among these deactivation pathways by probing their dependence on catalyst concentration. Specifically, increasing [cat] should amplify bimolecular deactivation (e.g., M18, M19) relative to unimolecular deactivation (M14) and alter the time-course curvature.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
The top candidate mechanisms involve various deactivation pathways: M11 (S+cat→inactive), M14 (catS→inactive), M16 (S+catS→inactive), M18 (2catS→inactive), M19 (cat+catS→inactive), M17 (P+catS→inactive), M12 (P+cat→inactive), M20 (combined cat and catS deactivation). To discriminate among them, we need to test how deactivation scales with catalyst concentration. Unimolecular deactivation (M14) scales linearly with [catS], while bimolecular deactivation (M18, M19, M11, M16) scales with higher powers of catalyst-containing species. By increasing [cat] to 0.15 M (15x higher than previous runs) while keeping [S]=2.0 M (same as run_1), we can compare the shape of the time course. If deactivation is bimolecular in catalyst species, the relative rate of deactivation versus turnover will increase at high [cat], leading to more pronounced curvature, earlier slowdown, and possibly lower final conversion. In contrast, unimolecular deactivation will show similar fractional conversion vs. time shape, just scaled in time. This experiment directly tests the molecularity of the deactivation step.
</hypothesis>
